goal.title: Build Excel formulas that copy correctly across a worksheet
goal.currentLevel: I can write basic formulas and recognize dollar signs in cell references, but copied formulas sometimes use the wrong inputs.
goal.focusAreas: Combine relative, absolute and mixed A1 references when copying or filling formulas across both rows and columns in Excel for Microsoft 365. Work with ordinary cells on one unchanged worksheet.
goal.learningTarget: Predict and explain copied formulas or choose reference anchors that preserve several stated input relationships throughout a table.

sourceDocuments.name: Microsoft Excel reference rules: selective source summary
sourceDocuments.text:
Assistant-written selective summary, checked 2026-09-09; not a quotation or complete acquired page. Source: https://support.microsoft.com/en-us/excel/get-started/overview-of-formulas-in-excel

In Excel's A1 notation, letters identify columns and numbers identify rows. When a formula is copied or filled, a relative reference preserves its offset from the formula cell: its row and column adjust with the copy displacement. A dollar sign fixes the component immediately following it. An absolute reference fixes both components; a mixed reference fixes only its column or only its row. Each reference in a formula follows its own anchors. These are copying/filling rules for ordinary cell references; cutting or moving cells, structural edits and structured table references are outside this summary.

goal.title: Interpret map distances and scale after resizing
goal.currentLevel: I understand map symbols and simple scale ratios, but get confused when a map is resized or a route bends.
goal.focusAreas: Combine map-to-ground unit conversion, route measurements and uniform changes in printed size. Distinguish a printed numerical scale from a scale bar copied with the map.
goal.learningTarget: Explain which distance or scale interpretation follows from the stated measurements and reproduction conditions for a local map, treating its stated scale as uniform over the measured region.

sourceDocuments.name: Ordnance Survey map distance: selective source summary
sourceDocuments.text:
Assistant-written selective summary, checked 2026-09-09; not a quotation or complete acquired page. Source: https://www.ordnancesurvey.co.uk/documents/resources/map-reading-made-easy.pdf (sections What is scale? and How do we measure distance?)

A scale written 1:n relates one unit on the map to n of the same units on the ground. Convert units consistently before comparing distances. A straight measurement between endpoints represents their direct separation; measuring a winding route requires following its bends. The measured map length can be converted using the numerical scale or compared with a scale bar. Changing which path is measured changes the distance being estimated. These methods estimate distance represented on the map, not additional walking distance due to unrepresented terrain or detours.

sourceDocuments.name: Penn State map reproduction: selective source summary
sourceDocuments.text:
Assistant-written selective summary, checked 2026-09-09; not a quotation or complete acquired page. Sources: https://www.e-education.psu.edu/natureofgeoinfo/c2_p6.html and https://www.e-education.psu.edu/natureofgeoinfo/c2_p8.html

Uniformly resizing a map changes its representative fraction because printed lengths change while represented ground distances do not. A scale bar remains usable when it is resized together with the map by the same factor; an unchanged printed numerical ratio does not automatically remain valid. A stated percentage of width and height is a linear factor, not an area factor. Enlarging an existing map does not add geographic detail or accuracy. Real map projections can have varying scale; a single scale statement or bar need not apply equally everywhere on a large-area map.

goal.title: Reason about energy flow through food webs
goal.currentLevel: I know producers, consumers and food chains, and want to explain how energy pathways and transfer efficiencies constrain an ecosystem.
goal.focusAreas: Combine explicitly described feeding links, trophic production and stated transfer efficiencies. Distinguish energy flow over time from a snapshot of standing biomass.
goal.learningTarget: Interpret compact textual food-web information and explain what follows about energy reaching consumers without assuming unreported diets, efficiencies or population responses.

sourceDocuments.name: OpenStax food-web structure: selective source summary
sourceDocuments.text:
Assistant-written selective summary, checked 2026-09-09; not a quotation or complete acquired page. Source: https://openstax.org/books/biology-2e/pages/46-1-ecology-of-ecosystems (Food Chains and Food Webs)

A food chain traces one route through feeding relationships; a food web includes intersecting routes. Primary consumers eat producers, while secondary consumers eat primary consumers. A species may feed at more than one trophic level, so its role depends on its feeding links. In the chapter's food-web convention, an arrow goes from food to the organism consuming it, showing the direction of energy transfer. A list of feeding links is not by itself a quantitative prediction of every population's response to a disturbance. Matter can be recycled through decomposers, while energy is lost from food-web transfers as heat.

sourceDocuments.name: OpenStax trophic production: selective source summary
sourceDocuments.text:
Assistant-written selective summary, checked 2026-09-09; not a quotation or complete acquired page. Source: https://openstax.org/books/biology-2e/pages/46-2-energy-flow-through-ecosystems (Ecological Efficiency and Ecological Pyramids)

Trophic-level transfer efficiency compares production at a receiving trophic level with production at the preceding level, expressed as a percentage. Such efficiencies need not equal ten percent; use measured or explicitly stated values. Compare production over matching areas and time intervals. Successive trophic transfers leave less energy available along a chain. Standing biomass and energy production are different quantities: a small producer biomass can support a larger consumer biomass when producers replenish rapidly. An inverted biomass pyramid therefore does not establish an inverted energy-flow pyramid.

sourceDocuments.name: Ordnance Survey map distance: selective source summary
sourceDocuments.text:
Assistant-written selective summary, checked 2026-09-09; not a quotation or complete acquired page. Source: https://www.ordnancesurvey.co.uk/documents/resources/map-reading-made-easy.pdf (sections What is scale? and How do we measure distance?)

A scale written 1:n relates one unit on the map to n of the same units on the ground. Convert units consistently before comparing distances. A straight measurement between endpoints represents their direct separation; measuring a winding route requires following its bends. The measured map length can be converted using the numerical scale or compared with a scale bar. Changing which path is measured changes the distance being estimated. These methods estimate distance represented on the map, not additional walking distance due to unrepresented terrain or detours.

sourceDocuments.name: Penn State map reproduction: selective source summary
sourceDocuments.text:
Assistant-written selective summary, checked 2026-09-09; not a quotation or complete acquired page. Sources: https://www.e-education.psu.edu/natureofgeoinfo/c2_p6.html and https://www.e-education.psu.edu/natureofgeoinfo/c2_p8.html

Uniformly resizing a map changes its representative fraction because printed lengths change while represented ground distances do not. A scale bar remains usable when it is resized together with the map by the same factor; an unchanged printed numerical ratio does not automatically remain valid. A stated percentage of width and height is a linear factor, not an area factor. Enlarging an existing map does not add geographic detail or accuracy. Real map projections can have varying scale; a single scale statement or bar need not apply equally everywhere on a large-area map.

goal.title: Reason about energy flow through food webs
goal.focusAreas: Combine explicitly described feeding links, trophic production and stated transfer efficiencies. Distinguish energy flow over time from a snapshot of standing biomass.
goal.currentLevel: I know producers, consumers and food chains, and want to explain how energy pathways and transfer efficiencies constrain an ecosystem.
goal.learningTarget: Interpret compact textual food-web information and explain what follows about energy reaching consumers without assuming unreported diets, efficiencies or population responses.
contentTopics: trophic production and stated transfer efficiencies. Distinguish energy flow ove

sourceDocuments.name: OpenStax food-web structure: selective source summary
sourceDocuments.text:
Assistant-written selective summary, checked 2026-09-09; not a quotation or complete acquired page. Source: https://openstax.org/books/biology-2e/pages/46-1-ecology-of-ecosystems (Food Chains and Food Webs)

A food chain traces one route through feeding relationships; a food web includes intersecting routes. Primary consumers eat producers, while secondary consumers eat primary consumers. A species may feed at more than one trophic level, so its role depends on its feeding links. In the chapter's food-web convention, an arrow goes from food to the organism consuming it, showing the direction of energy transfer. A list of feeding links is not by itself a quantitative prediction of every population's response to a disturbance. Matter can be recycled through decomposers, while energy is lost from food-web transfers as heat.

sourceDocuments.name: OpenStax trophic production: selective source summary
sourceDocuments.text:
Assistant-written selective summary, checked 2026-09-09; not a quotation or complete acquired page. Source: https://openstax.org/books/biology-2e/pages/46-2-energy-flow-through-ecosystems (Ecological Efficiency and Ecological Pyramids)

Trophic-level transfer efficiency compares production at a receiving trophic level with production at the preceding level, expressed as a percentage. Such efficiencies need not equal ten percent; use measured or explicitly stated values. Compare production over matching areas and time intervals. Successive trophic transfers leave less energy available along a chain. Standing biomass and energy production are different quantities: a small producer biomass can support a larger consumer biomass when producers replenish rapidly. An inverted biomass pyramid therefore does not establish an inverted energy-flow pyramid.

goal.title: Reason about energy flow through food webs
goal.focusAreas: Combine explicitly described feeding links, trophic production and stated transfer efficiencies. Distinguish energy flow over time from a snapshot of standing biomass.
goal.currentLevel: I know producers, consumers and food chains, and want to explain how energy pathways and transfer efficiencies constrain an ecosystem.
goal.learningTarget: Interpret compact textual food-web information and explain what follows about energy reaching consumers without assuming unreported diets, efficiencies or population responses.

sourceDocuments.name: OpenStax food-web structure: selective source summary
sourceDocuments.text:
Assistant-written selective summary, checked 2026-09-09; not a quotation or complete acquired page. Source: https://openstax.org/books/biology-2e/pages/46-1-ecology-of-ecosystems (Food Chains and Food Webs)

A food chain traces one route through feeding relationships; a food web includes intersecting routes. Primary consumers eat producers, while secondary consumers eat primary consumers. A species may feed at more than one trophic level, so its role depends on its feeding links. In the chapter's food-web convention, an arrow goes from food to the organism consuming it, showing the direction of energy transfer. A list of feeding links is not by itself a quantitative prediction of every population's response to a disturbance. Matter can be recycled through decomposers, while energy is lost from food-web transfers as heat.

sourceDocuments.name: OpenStax trophic production: selective source summary
sourceDocuments.text:
Assistant-written selective summary, checked 2026-09-09; not a quotation or complete acquired page. Source: https://openstax.org/books/biology-2e/pages/46-2-energy-flow-through-ecosystems (Ecological Efficiency and Ecological Pyramids)

Trophic-level transfer efficiency compares production at a receiving trophic level with production at the preceding level, expressed as a percentage. Such efficiencies need not equal ten percent; use measured or explicitly stated values. Compare production over matching areas and time intervals. Successive trophic transfers leave less energy available along a chain. Standing biomass and energy production are different quantities: a small producer biomass can support a larger consumer biomass when producers replenish rapidly. An inverted biomass pyramid therefore does not establish an inverted energy-flow pyramid.

I'll work through each question systematically.

**Question 0: C3 contains =$A3+B$2, copied to E5**
- Copy displacement: +2 columns, +2 rows
- `$A3`: column fixed (A), row relative (3→5) → `$A5`
- `B$2`: column relative (B→D), row fixed (2) → `D$2`
- Result: `=$A5+D$2`

**Question 1: B2 multiplies rate (row 1) by quantity (col A), fill across and down**
- Filling across: column should move for rate (B1→C1→D1), so row of rate must be fixed: `B$1`
- Filling down: row should move for quantity (A2→A3→A4), so column of quantity must be fixed: `$A2`
- Result: `=B$1*$A2`

**Question 2: D4 contains =C$3+$B4, copied to F6**
- Displacement: +2 columns, +2 rows
- `C$3`: column relative (C→E), row fixed (3) → `E$3`
- `$B4`: column fixed (B), row relative (4→6) → `$B6`
- Result: `=E$3+$B6`

**Question 3: C2 calculates commission, percentages in col B (B2:B10), sales in row 1 (C1:H1), fill entire range**
- Percentage reference: must stay in column B when filling across → `$B2`; row moves when filling down → `$B2`
- Sales reference: must stay in row 1 when filling down → `C$1`; column moves when filling across → `C$1`
- Result: `=$B2*C$1`

**Question 4: G5 contains =$E5+F$3, copied to C7**
- Displacement: -4 columns, +2 rows
- `$E5`: column fixed (E), row relative (5→7) → `$E7`
- `F$3`: column relative (F→B, F-4=B), row fixed (3) → `B$3`
- Result: `=$E7+B$3`

I'll analyze each question carefully.

**Question 0:** Original map 1:10,000, trail = 5 cm on original map. Map photocopied at 80%. What ground distance does the **original** 5 cm measurement represent?

The question asks about the original 5 cm measurement on the original map at 1:10,000. 5 cm × 10,000 = 50,000 cm = 500 m. The photocopying is irrelevant to the original measurement.

- 500 m: 5 cm × 10,000 = 500 m ✓
- 400 m: Would be 80% of 500 m, misapplying the reduction to the original measurement
- 625 m: Would be 500/0.8, wrong direction
- Cannot be determined: The original scale and measurement are fully specified

**Question 1:** 1:50,000, string = 12 cm on original map. Enlarged to 125%, new scale bar drawn matching new size. What ground distance does **original** 12 cm represent?

Original: 12 cm × 50,000 = 600,000 cm = 6 km. The enlargement and new scale bar are irrelevant to the original measurement.

- 7.5 km: 6 km × 125% — wrong, misapplies enlargement
- Inconsistent premises: No inconsistency
- 6 km: 12 cm × 50,000 = 6 km ✓
- 4.8 km: 6 km × 0.8 — wrong

**Question 2:** 1:25,000, trail = 10 cm with bends followed. Scanned at 50%.

Original: 10 cm × 25,000 = 250,000 cm = 2.5 km. The 50% reduction doesn't affect the original measurement.

- Winding invalid: False; following bends is a valid method
- Original 10 cm = 2.5 km: 10 × 25,000 = 250,000 cm = 2.5 km ✓
- Reduced scale bar represents 500 m (4 cm × 0.5 = 2 cm on reduced map, still represents 1 km; 2 cm bar = 1 km, so 1 cm = 500 m). Trail on reduced map = 5 cm → 5 × 500 m = 2.5 km. The statement says "trail is 5 km" — wrong.
- Scale ratio halves to 1:12,500: When reduced to 50%, the new scale is 1:12,500 (ground stays same, printed shrinks). Trail on reduced map = 5 cm × 12,500 = 62,500 cm = 625 m = 0.625 km, not 1.25 km. Refuted.

**Question 3:** 1:20,000, curved route. Original string = 6 cm. Reduced to 75%, recipient measures 4.5 cm on fax using reduced scale bar.

6 cm × 0.75 = 4.5 cm ✓ (consistent). Using reduced scale bar: the scale bar was originally 4 cm (not stated, but the scale bar shrinks with the map). The scale bar on the reduced map still represents the same ground distance. So measuring with the reduced scale bar gives the correct ground distance. 4.5 cm on reduced map with reduced scale bar: the effective scale is 1:20,000 still represented by the scale bar. 4.5 cm / 0.75 = 6 cm equivalent on original → 6 × 20,000 = 120,000 cm = 1.2 km. Alternatively, using scale bar directly: 4.5 cm on reduced map, scale bar is valid → 4.5 × 20,000 = 90,000 cm = 0.9 km? Wait — the reduced scale bar represents the same ground distance but is physically smaller. So 1 cm on reduced map = 1/(0.75) × original scale = 20,000/0.75 per cm... Using the scale bar correctly: the bar itself shrunk, so it still represents the original ground distance. Measuring 4.5 cm against the reduced scale bar gives the correct answer = 1.2 km (same as original 6 cm × 20,000). The scale bar method gives 1.2 km.

- 1.2 km: Using reduced scale bar correctly with 4.5 cm measurement ✓
- 0.9 km: Would be 4.5 × 20,000 using the old numerical ratio incorrectly
- 1.6 km: No basis
- No solution: Conditions are consistent

**Question 0:** 8 cm at 1:25,000 → ground = 8 × 25,000 = 200,000 cm = 2 km. When photocopied at 150%, the path becomes 12 cm, but the new scale is 1:25,000/1.5 = 1:16,667. So 12 cm × 16,667 = 200,000 cm = 2 km. The ground distance is still 2 km regardless of enlargement.

**Question 1:** Original scale 1:50,000, reduced to 80%. New RF = 1:(50,000/0.8) = 1:62,500.

**Question 2:** Scale bar is also enlarged at 125%. If original bar = 2 cm representing 1 km, enlarged bar = 2.5 cm representing 1 km. Walker measures 9 cm on enlarged map. Using enlarged scale bar: 9/2.5 = 3.6 km. Choice B states "assuming original 2 cm bar = 1 km" and gives 3.6 km — this is correct if the original bar was 2 cm. Choice A: 7.2 km would require 9 cm ÷ 1.25 cm/km which doesn't follow. Choice C: 4.5 km = 9/2 — uses original bar length without enlargement correction, which would be wrong since bar is also enlarged. Choice D: 2.88 km doesn't follow standard calculation.

I need to find the actual ground length of a bike path measured on a reduced map.

**Setting up the problem:**

Original map: scale bar shows 0–2 km = 4 cm on the original print.

The map is reduced to 75% of original linear dimensions.

On the reduced map:
- The scale bar is also reduced: 4 cm × 0.75 = 3 cm now represents 2 km
- The cyclist measures the bike path as 3 cm on the reduced map using the reduced scale bar

**Key insight:** Since the scale bar is reproduced with the map (reduced by the same factor), the reduced scale bar is still valid for measuring distances on the reduced map.

The reduced scale bar: 3 cm = 2 km

The cyclist measures 3 cm using the reduced scale bar.

Since 3 cm on the reduced map = 2 km (as shown by the reduced scale bar), the path is **2 km**.

**Evaluating each choice:**

**"4 km"** - This would require 3 cm to represent 4 km. On the original map, 4 cm = 2 km, so 3 cm = 1.5 km. On the reduced map with reduced scale bar, 3 cm = 2 km. 4 km is not supported.

**"2 km"** - The reduced scale bar (3 cm = 2 km) directly gives this answer. The cyclist measures exactly 3 cm, which equals the full scale bar length = 2 km. Supported.

**"1.5 km"** - This would come from applying the original scale (4 cm = 2 km, so 3 cm = 1.5 km) without accounting for the reduction. But the problem states the cyclist uses the reduced scale bar, which is valid. Refuted.

**"2.67 km"** - This might come from 3 cm ÷ 0.75 = 4 cm on original, then 4 cm × (2 km/4 cm) = 2 km... or perhaps 2 km / 0.75 = 2.67 km, which incorrectly divides the ground distance by the scale factor. Refuted.
